nodes.chainStep: Airway, breathing and blood pressure first, treating anaphylaxis before anything else; full vital signs with temperature; examine all the skin, the conjunctivae, mouth and genitals, noting whether spots blanch; list every drug started in the last 8 weeks
nodes.why: Hives or swelling of acute onset with breathing trouble, low blood pressure or severe gut symptoms is anaphylaxis, and epinephrine comes before any skin diagnosis. In suspected sepsis the skin is examined for mottling, cyanosis and a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, and when meningococcal disease is possible all of the body is checked, the conjunctivae included, because rashes are harder to see on brown, black or tanned skin. The mouth, eyes and genitals are examined because mucosal involvement is the hallmark of SJS/TEN, and the drug history reaches back 8 weeks because SJS/TEN appears within 8 weeks of starting a drug. A biopsy confirms several of these diagnoses, but never before the airway, breathing and pressure, and a rash photographed before the vital signs leaves anaphylaxis and shock untreated.

Hydrocortisone is not a first-hour drug here: corticosteroids are not routine in meningococcal disease, low-dose replacement being kept for septic shock that does not respond to high-dose vasoactive drugs, and they are not recommended as adjuncts in toxic shock syndrome.

nodes.why: Ceftriaxone is the antibiotic for suspected or confirmed meningococcal disease in hospital. A lumbar puncture is not done with extensive or rapidly spreading purpura, so it does not confirm the organism here; the throat swab, blood culture and whole-blood PCR do that work. Droplet precautions continue for at least 24 hours after effective antibiotics start, not just past the first dose, and close contacts get chemoprophylaxis rather than waiting for a fever. Corticosteroids are not routine in meningococcal disease; dexamethasone is the bacterial meningitis drug when meningitis is strongly suspected, stopped once the organism is meningococcus, and low-dose replacement steroids are kept for septic shock that does not respond to high-dose vasoactive drugs.

nodes.why: Any source of toxin, such as a tampon or nasal packing, comes out at once, and a soft tissue source, necrotizing fasciitis above all, needs emergency surgery. Until the organism is known the regimen is broad, usually with vancomycin or linezolid for MRSA plus gram-negative cover, and clindamycin is added because it suppresses toxin production; it is bacteriostatic, so it is never given alone, and waiting for group A streptococcus to grow delays the antitoxin effect. Corticosteroids are not recommended as adjuncts in toxic shock syndrome.

nodes.why: Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for rickettsial disease in adults and children, and early treatment is the strongest determinant of outcome: untreated RMSF can kill 20% to 30%. It starts on suspicion, because IgG is often undetectable in the first week and a negative early result does not exclude the disease. Children under 8 get it too: short courses do not cause clinically significant tooth staining, and the risk from delayed treatment is far greater. Macrolides and chloramphenicol are inferior alternatives for when doxycycline cannot be used, and fluoroquinolones are linked to worse outcomes.

ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and infections such as HIV and hepatitis C cause secondary ITP.

nodes.summary: Adults with platelets of 30 or more and no or minor bleeding: observation rather than corticosteroids, as outpatients, with hematology in 24 to 72 hours; steroids may suit a low count, comorbidity, anticoagulants or antiplatelets, a procedure, or age over 60. Children with skin-only bleeding: observation; non-life-threatening mucosal bleeding: prednisone 2 to 4 mg/kg a day (maximum 120 mg) for 5 to 7 days rather than IVIG.

Adult ITP with platelets under 30 and minor bleeding: a short course of prednisone or dexamethasone, admission when under 20 at diagnosis, and a search for secondary causes; children with no or minor bleeding are observed instead. Critical bleeding gets platelets with IVIG and steroids.

DIC: treat the cause (sepsis, an obstetric emergency, trauma or cancer). Platelets and plasma only for bleeding, a high bleeding risk or a procedure: platelets under 50 when bleeding, under 10 to 20 at high risk without bleeding; fresh frozen plasma 15 to 30 mL/kg and cryoprecipitate replace factors; prophylactic heparin or LMWH when not bleeding. Fever with DIC and purpura follows the meningococcal route.

nodes.ask: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, platelets and clotting normal. Next?
options: Urinalysis, blood pressure and creatinine; review recent drugs and infections
A repeat platelet count in a week, and no other tests while the count stays normal
Skin biopsy first; urine and pressure once the biopsy shows IgA deposits
Clotting factor assays and a bleeding work-up, since the spots are purpuric
nodes.chainStep: Urinalysis (protein to creatinine ratio if protein is present), blood pressure and creatinine at diagnosis; recent drugs, infections and vaccines; skin biopsy with DIF when the cause is unclear; in a child with IgA vasculitis, urinalysis weekly for 4 to 6 weeks, then monthly to 6 months
nodes.why: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks with a normal platelet count is small vessel vasculitis, and the kidney decides the urgency: children with IgA vasculitis need urinalysis at diagnosis and repeatedly for 6 months, and blood pressure at diagnosis. The common triggers are drugs (beta-lactams, NSAIDs, allopurinol, sulfonamides and others) and preceding infections, so removing the trigger is treatment. A skin biopsy with DIF confirms it, but it does not replace the urine and pressure check; the bleeding into the skin comes from inflamed small vessels (red cell extravasation on biopsy), so with normal clotting a bleeding work-up adds nothing.

orders.dose: Urinalysis frequently for 6 months (weekly for the first 4 to 6 weeks, then monthly); blood pressure at diagnosis and with nephritis
Severe gut involvement, significant nephritis (protein to creatinine ratio over 250 mg/mmol, nephrotic or nephritic syndrome, kidney insufficiency), CNS involvement or pulmonary hemorrhage
Antibiotics including beta-lactams, NSAIDs, allopurinol, sulfonamides, thiazides, phenytoin, quinolones, propylthiouracil; preceding infections; screen for hepatitis B and C, HIV and endocarditis
With DIF; H&E of a lesion under 48 hours old, DIF of one under 24 hours old
Blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel, liver tests, urinalysis, and a urine protein to creatinine ratio if protein is present

nodes.summary: Cutaneous small vessel vasculitis: remove the trigger (stop a suspect drug, treat an infection); most idiopathic cases settle within weeks to months. IgA vasculitis in a child: urinalysis weekly for 4 to 6 weeks and then monthly to 6 months, blood pressure checks, specialist advice for significant nephritis, severe gut involvement, CNS signs or pulmonary hemorrhage, and corticosteroids considered for severe abdominal pain or GI bleeding once intussusception is excluded.

Non-blanching spots with a normal count, film and clotting and no spread: with fever, the antibiotics continue and a senior decides on admission, because normal blood tests do not rule out meningococcal disease. Afebrile and well with an obvious cause, such as trauma or spots confined above the nipple line, observation is enough, and the person goes home if nothing spreads, told to return if the rash spreads or changes or new symptoms appear.

nodes.ask: Widespread blisters or peeling skin. What decides the route?
options: Mouth, eyes and genitals; Nikolsky sign; the skin area lost; drugs in the last 8 weeks
A swab of the blister fluid for culture first; the full examination once it is reported
The itch and the age; mucosa and drug history once the blisters spread further
Viral PCR of the blister fluid; the drug list reviewed if the PCR is negative
nodes.chainStep: Examine the mouth, eyes and genitals; test the Nikolsky sign; estimate detached skin as a share of body surface; list every drug started in the last 8 weeks; blood count, clotting, urea, electrolytes, bicarbonate, glucose and liver tests; urgent skin biopsy (frozen section) and a perilesional biopsy for DIF
nodes.why: Mucosal involvement is the hallmark of SJS/TEN, present in 90% and often 1 to 3 days before the skin, while the inside of the mouth is spared in staphylococcal scalded skin and classic bullous pemphigoid spares the mucosa. A positive Nikolsky sign marks detaching epidermis in SJS/TEN and in scalded skin. The detached area grades SJS (under 10%), overlap (10% to 30%) and TEN (over 30%) and enters SCORTEN, and the drug history covers 8 weeks because that is when SJS/TEN appears. Blister fluid cultures are typically negative in scalded skin, and waiting for any result delays stopping a culprit drug.

orders.dose: Involved in 90% of SJS/TEN, often 1 to 3 days before the skin; the inside of the mouth is spared in scalded skin; classic bullous pemphigoid has no mucosal involvement
SJS under 10% of body surface; SJS-TEN overlap 10% to 30%; TEN over 30%
Urgent frozen section shows full-thickness necrosis in SJS/TEN, with negative DIF; DIF for pemphigoid is taken from perilesional skin, not a blister
Blood count, ESR, clotting, urea and electrolytes and liver tests, for supportive care, organ failure and prognosis

Pemphigoid pattern; older, itchy tense blisters, mouth spared
Other blisters; impetigo, burns, contact or bite blisters

nodes.ask: Acute mucosal erosions and detaching skin, usually after a new drug. First?
options: Stop every suspect drug now; SCORTEN within 24 hours; a burn unit or ICU early
Stop the likeliest drug and keep the others until patch testing names the culprit
Start prophylactic IV antibiotics for the open skin; stop drugs once the biopsy is back
Keep the drugs while a test dose confirms the culprit; then a specialist unit
nodes.chainStep: Stop all suspect drugs now and never restart them; SCORTEN on day 1 and again on day 3; early transfer to a burn unit or ICU experienced in SJS/TEN; skin swabs on day 1 and every 48 hours; no prophylactic antibiotics
nodes.why: In the ED two measures matter most: stopping the offending drug and early referral to a burn unit or ICU experienced in the disease; done within 24 hours of blistering, they lower the infection rate and improve survival. SCORTEN is scored in the first 24 hours and again on day 3. Rechallenge is contraindicated, so no drug is kept or test-dosed to find the culprit, and patch testing is only an adjunct. Prophylactic antibiotics do not change survival; skin swabs on day 1 and every 48 hours find the infection that needs treatment.

orders.dose: Stop it, with early referral to a burn unit or ICU; within 24 hours of blistering, these lower infection and improve survival
Contraindicated in SJS and TEN

1 point each: age over 40, heart rate 120 or more, cancer, detachment of 10% or more of body surface on day 1, BUN over 28 mg/dL, bicarbonate under 20, glucose over 252 mg/dL; within 24 hours, repeated on day 3
Not recommended; swab the skin on day 1 and every 48 hours and treat infection, rapid deterioration or a sudden fall in temperature

nodes.ask: SJS/TEN, the suspect drugs stopped. Supportive care?
options: Warmed room, nonadherent dressings, fluids by urine output, opioids, early ophthalmology
Warmed room, nonadherent dressings, fluids, and prophylactic IV antibiotics for the open skin
Warmed room, nonadherent dressings, fluids, opioids; ophthalmology once the skin has healed
Ward care with daily dermatology input; transfer if the SCORTEN rises on day 3
nodes.chainStep: Prevent hypothermia; nonadherent dressings, leaving detached epidermis in place; crystalloid to a MAP over 65 mm Hg and urine output 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h; opioid analgesia; enteral nutrition; early ophthalmology (within 24 hours in one guideline); genital mucosal care; systemic immunomodulation only as a specialist decision
nodes.why: Supportive care until the skin heals is the mainstay: fluids guided by perfusion and urine output, pain control, wound care with nonadherent dressings, warmth against hypothermia, and nutrition. The eyes need ophthalmology early, because ocular complications are common and sometimes serious; one guideline sets the review within the first 24 hours, so waiting for the skin to heal is too late. Prophylactic antibiotics do not change survival, and transfer is early, not saved for a rising score. Systemic corticosteroids, ciclosporin and IVIG have no proven benefit and the sources disagree on them, so they are not an ED order.

orders.dose: StatPearls: crystalloid by a burn protocol such as Parkland, to a MAP over 65 mm Hg, CVP 8 to 12 mm Hg and urine output 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h
orders.note: The 2026 pediatric consensus found no agreement on burns-based requirements and advises individualized fluids by volume status, urine output and biochemistry, not a fixed burns formula.

orders.dose: Early ophthalmology, with lubricants and topical antibiotic or steroid drops as directed; one guideline sets the review within the first 24 hours
Nonadherent dressings; detached epidermis left in place as a natural dressing
Enteral rather than parenteral, 20 to 25 kcal/kg a day
A specialist decision, not an ED order
orders.note: StatPearls: no proven treatment, and some studies link corticosteroids to higher mortality; EuroSCAR found no benefit from corticosteroids or IVIG over supportive care; an Indian review favors early dexamethasone and ciclosporin 3 mg/kg a day; 4 of 10 pediatric guidelines recommend systemic corticosteroids and 5 of 10 IVIG; the review's synthesis says consider early corticosteroids case by case.

orders.dose: Not recommended; they do not change survival

sources.where: Results: supportive care; multidisciplinary care; ocular care

nodes.summary: SJS/TEN: every suspect drug stopped and never restarted, SCORTEN in the first 24 hours and again on day 3, early transfer to a burn unit or ICU, early ophthalmology and supportive care; systemic immunomodulation is a specialist decision because the evidence conflicts.

nodes.ask: Child, fever, tender red skin peeling with a positive Nikolsky sign, mouth spared. Next?
options: Admit; IV antistaphylococcal antibiotic, fluids and skin care; no NSAIDs
Admit; IV antistaphylococcal antibiotic and ibuprofen for the fever and pain
Oral clindamycin alone as an outpatient, to switch off the toxin
Stop recent drugs and transfer to a burn unit as SJS/TEN, with IV immunoglobulin
nodes.chainStep: Admit (ICU if extensive); IV nafcillin or oxacillin 100 to 150 mg/kg a day divided every 6 hours, or cefazolin 50 to 100 mg/kg a day divided every 8 hours; vancomycin if MRSA is likely; emollients and nonadherent dressings; fluids and temperature control; paracetamol or opioids, no NSAIDs, no silver sulfadiazine; about 10 days in all
nodes.why: Severe, generalized scalded skin needs admission and IV antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus, with fluids, warmth and wound care, because the lost epidermis leaks fluid and heat. NSAIDs are avoided for the risk of kidney impairment. Clindamycin may cut toxin production, but up to 50% of strains are resistant, so it is never used alone. The inside of the mouth is spared, which separates scalded skin from SJS/TEN, a drug reaction with mucosal erosions.

orders.dose: Nafcillin or oxacillin 100 to 150 mg/kg a day divided every 6 hours, or cefazolin 50 to 100 mg/kg a day divided every 8 hours
Vancomycin: recent healthcare exposure or high local MRSA prevalence
An oral beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin or first-generation cephalosporin for at least 1 week
May reduce toxin production, but up to 50% of strains are resistant: not as monotherapy
Avoid: risk of kidney impairment
Avoid: systemic absorption and toxicity
10 days unless clinical judgment says longer

nodes.summary: Not in this version: bullous impetigo, burns, contact and bite blisters. Scalded skin in an adult, usually with kidney failure or immunocompromise, is treated as on the scalded skin route.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: admission, IV antistaphylococcal antibiotics (vancomycin when MRSA is likely), fluids, warmth and gentle skin care, and no NSAIDs; the inside of the mouth is spared, and children usually heal with little or no scarring.

nodes.ask: Weeks of mouth erosions, now flaccid blisters, no new drug. Next?
options: Lesional and perilesional biopsies with DIF; dermatology; systemic corticosteroids
Clobetasol 0.05% cream as first-line treatment, with a biopsy if blisters keep forming
A 5-day prednisolone burst without a biopsy, then a clinic visit in a month
Stop her regular medicines and transfer to a burn unit for presumed TEN
nodes.chainStep: Biopsy a fresh lesion for histology and perilesional skin for DIF; desmoglein serology (ELISA or IIF); dermatology; systemic corticosteroids, with rituximab (anti-CD20) first-line for moderate to severe disease; ask about penicillamine, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and cephalosporins
nodes.why: Pemphigus is confirmed by a compatible clinical picture and histology plus either a positive DIF of perilesional skin or serum autoantibodies against the epithelial cell surface, so a burst without a biopsy skips the diagnosis. Systemic corticosteroids are the backbone, they take several weeks to work, and an anti-CD20 antibody such as rituximab joins them first-line for moderate to severe disease. A superpotent topical steroid as first-line is the pemphigoid approach. SJS/TEN is a drug reaction; only about 5% have no recent drug.

orders.dose: Clinical picture and histology, plus a positive DIF of perilesional skin or serum autoantibodies against the epithelial cell surface
Systemic corticosteroids; an anti-CD20 antibody such as rituximab with them for moderate to severe disease
Not extracted: the panel's dosing table and the EADV and BAD guidelines were not read, and StatPearls gives no dose
D-penicillamine, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and cephalosporins

nodes.summary: Pemphigus vulgaris: lesional and perilesional biopsies with DIF or serology, dermatology, systemic corticosteroids, and rituximab with them for moderate to severe disease; the response takes weeks.

nodes.ask: Older adult, itchy tense blisters on the trunk and limbs, mouth spared. Next?
options: Perilesional biopsy for DIF; clobetasol 0.05% cream first-line; dermatology
IV methylprednisolone pulses and rituximab as the first-line treatment
Oral prednisone 2 mg/kg a day as first-line, tapered off over the next 2 weeks
Stop his regular medicines and transfer to a burn unit as for toxic epidermal necrolysis
nodes.chainStep: Perilesional biopsy (not a blister) for DIF in Michel medium or saline, plus histology; anti-BP180 and BP230 serology; clobetasol propionate 0.05% cream once or twice daily, up to 20 g a day, sparing the face and folds; prednisone 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day when topical treatment is not practical; doxycycline 200 mg a day may be added
nodes.why: Classic bullous pemphigoid is intensely itchy with tense blisters, typically after 70 and with the mucosa spared, and DIF of perilesional skin, not a blister, shows linear IgG or C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction. Clobetasol propionate 0.05% is first-line where it is practical: against oral prednisone it controlled more patients at 3 weeks with fewer severe adverse events and lower mortality. When topical treatment is impractical, prednisone is 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day, tapered slowly over 6 to 9 months or longer, not over 2 weeks; rituximab is for resistant disease. With the mouth spared, tense blisters and no new drug, this is not toxic epidermal necrolysis.

orders.dose: Clinical picture and histology with DIF showing linear IgG or C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction, or positive serology
First-line where appropriate, once or twice daily up to 20 g a day, sparing the face and folds
orders.note: StatPearls makes systemic corticosteroids the mainstay and keeps clobetasol for localized disease under 20% of the body surface in the elderly; the Canadian consensus makes clobetasol first-line wherever topical treatment is practical.

orders.dose: 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day when topical treatment is not practical
Slowly, over 6 to 9 months or longer
200 mg a day can be added throughout treatment
Azathioprine, mycophenolate or methotrexate; IVIG, rituximab or omalizumab when the others fail

nodes.summary: Bullous pemphigoid: perilesional DIF with linear IgG or C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction, superpotent topical clobetasol first-line, prednisone 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day when topical treatment is impractical, and dermatology follow-up for a taper over months.

nodes.ask: Target lesions. What separates erythema multiforme from SJS?
options: Raised 3-ring targets on the limbs vs flat dusky 2-ring targets on the trunk
Mouth erosions mean SJS; targets without mouth sores mean erythema multiforme
A recent cold sore means SJS; a new drug points to erythema multiforme instead
Itchy targets mean erythema multiforme; painless ones mean SJS
nodes.chainStep: Look at shape and site: typical raised targets with 3 zones, under 3 cm, acral and symmetric (erythema multiforme) vs atypical flat 2-zone purpuric targets, mainly on the trunk, with blisters and detachment (SJS); check the mucosa and the detached area; ask about cold sores, mycoplasma and new drugs
nodes.why: Erythema multiforme has typical targets with 3 concentric zones, under 3 cm, mainly acral and symmetric, and about 90% follow an infection, herpes simplex most often. SJS lacks typical targets: its target-like lesions have 2 zones, turn purpuric, sit mainly on the trunk and come with detachment, and a drug is usually the cause. The mouth does not separate them, because significant mucosal involvement defines erythema multiforme major, and typical erythema multiforme lesions do not itch, while SJS erosions are painful.

orders.dose: Round lesions with 3 concentric zones, under 3 cm, mainly acral and symmetric; about 90% triggered by infection, herpes simplex most often
No typical targets: asymmetric target-like lesions with 2 zones that turn purpuric, mainly axial, usually from a drug

outcomes.if: Erythema multiforme; raised 3-ring targets on the limbs, no detachment
SJS pattern; flat dusky targets on the trunk, blisters, a new drug

nodes.summary: Erythema multiforme: remove and treat the trigger (aciclovir or valacyclovir if herpes is suspected, antibiotics for mycoplasma), supportive mouth and lip care, ophthalmology for eye involvement, and admission for severe pain, dehydration or poor intake. Recurrent herpes-associated attacks are suppressed with aciclovir 400 mg or valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for at least 6 months.

nodes.ask: Widespread red rash, no blisters, not in shock. Next?
options: Fever, mucosa, nodes, facial swelling; eosinophils, liver and kidney tests
An oral antihistamine now; blood tests if the rash lasts beyond a week
Oral prednisolone for 5 days, started before the blood tests are taken
A skin biopsy first, with the blood tests once the histology is reported
nodes.chainStep: Temperature; mouth, eyes and lymph nodes; facial swelling; share of skin involved; blood count with differential (eosinophils, atypical lymphocytes), liver and kidney tests; every drug started in the last 8 weeks
nodes.why: A drug rash needs admission when the skin signs are severe (over 60% of the skin, confluent redness, facial swelling, mucosal erosions, blisters), with high fever, lymphadenopathy or hypotension, or when the bloods show eosinophils over 1,000 per mm3, atypical lymphocytes or abnormal liver tests. Those are the features of DRESS, which appears weeks after the drug, and the bloods show its eosinophilia and organ injury, so an antihistamine with the bloods put off for a week misses it. Oral corticosteroids are often used for drug rashes but have no proven efficacy, and a biopsy does not replace the blood tests.

orders.dose: Skin over 60%, confluent redness, facial edema, skin pain, palpable purpura, necrosis, blisters or detachment, Nikolsky sign, mucosal erosions; high fever, nodes, arthritis, dyspnea, hypotension; eosinophils over 1,000 per mm3, atypical lymphocytes, abnormal liver tests
WAO 2024: usually 2 to 8 weeks after the drug
orders.note: StatPearls (Cutaneous Adverse Drug Reaction) gives 2 to 6 weeks.

orders.dose: 2 to 3 possible, 4 to 5 probable, over 5 definite
The scoring items sit in a supplement (Figure S3) that was not read

1 day to 3 weeks after the drug, no mucosal involvement, starting on the trunk and spreading symmetrically

Erythroderma, no DRESS features; red over 90% of the skin
Rash only; afebrile, well, mucosa spared, normal bloods

nodes.ask: Fever and a widespread spotty rash, no new drug. First move?
options: A side room until measles is excluded; then eyes, mouth, nodes, hands and feet
The open waiting room until seen, since most of these rashes are viral
A throat swab first, with a side room if it is negative for group A strep
Bloods for eosinophils and liver enzymes before deciding where the patient waits
nodes.chainStep: Isolate on arrival in a side room as a possible measles case; ask about vaccination and contacts; look for cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and white buccal spots (measles), a sore throat with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue (scarlet fever), and 5 or more days of fever with conjunctival injection, red lips or tongue, swollen red hands and feet and a cervical node (Kawasaki disease)
nodes.why: Anyone with fever and a rash is potentially infectious, so the patient goes to a side room on arrival rather than the waiting room, and a suspected measles case is notified and isolated without waiting for a test. The rest of the look sorts the three ED flags: the 3 Cs with buccal spots for measles, a sore throat with the sandpaper rash for scarlet fever, and at least 5 days of fever with 4 of the 5 criteria for Kawasaki disease. A throat swab or blood tests come after isolation, not before.

orders.dose: Doxycycline now, as on the rickettsial route, whether or not the spots blanch; never delayed for tests

sources.where: History and physical; Treatment / management; Differential diagnosis

orders.dose: Isolate on arrival; inform infection control; notify the health protection team as soon as it is suspected; supportive care; vitamin A daily for 2 days (WHO, AAP)

Penicillin V or amoxicillin by mouth for 10 days, or one IM dose of benzathine penicillin G; a macrolide or clindamycin for allergy, by local resistance; away from nursery, school or work until 24 hours after starting

Fever 5 days or more with 4 of 5: bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; red mouth, strawberry tongue or cracked lips; polymorphous rash; red, swollen hands and feet; a cervical node over 1.5 cm. IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours with aspirin, ideally within 7 to 10 days of fever onset
StatPearls 2023: 80 to 100 mg/kg a day divided every 6 hours until afebrile for over 48 hours, then 3 to 5 mg/kg a day
orders.note: The 2024 AHA scientific statement is in an LWW journal (barred) and was not read.

nodes.ask: Rash weeks after a new drug, with fever, eosinophilia or organ injury. Next?
options: Stop the drug, admit, treat by severity; a systemic steroid tapers over 2 to 3 months
Stop the drug; a 5-day oral prednisolone burst as an outpatient, with no taper after
Stop the drug; IV immunoglobulin as first-line in place of corticosteroids, on the ward
Continue the drug at a lower dose, with an antihistamine and weekly liver tests
nodes.chainStep: Stop the culprit drug for good; admit; score RegiSCAR and repeat the blood count, liver, kidney and other organ tests; moderate or severe DRESS: prednisolone or equivalent 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day, tapered over 2 to 3 months; a possible case (RegiSCAR 2 to 3): a moderate-potency topical steroid and close follow-up (EAACI, children); ciclosporin, IVIG or other agents for steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent disease
nodes.why: Withdrawing the offending drug immediately, with supportive care, comes first, and systemic corticosteroids are the standard treatment for moderate and severe DRESS: prednisolone 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day, tapered over 2 to 3 months. A possible case without organ injury (RegiSCAR 2 to 3) gets a moderate-potency topical steroid with supportive care and close follow-up in the EAACI pediatric paper. A rapid reduction can cause severe or fatal flares and relapses, so a 5-day burst is wrong. IVIG, ciclosporin and other agents are for steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent disease or when steroids are contraindicated, not first-line, and the drug is never continued.

orders.dose: Withdraw it immediately, with supportive therapy
Prednisolone or equivalent 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day for moderate and severe DRESS, tapered over 2 to 3 months
Can cause severe or fatal flares or relapses
Moderate-potency topical corticosteroid, supportive care and close follow-up for progression (EAACI, children)
Immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin, IVIG, biologics or plasmapheresis

nodes.ask: Red, scaling skin over 90% of the body, not in shock, no organ injury. Next?
options: Admit; fluids, warmth, electrolytes; emollients, wet dressings, mild topical steroid
A potent topical steroid as an outpatient, with dermatology to follow
IV antibiotics from the start, because the lost skin barrier invites infection
A skin biopsy first; treatment starts once the histology names the cause
nodes.chainStep: Admit when severe; monitor hemodynamics, temperature, fluid balance, electrolytes and albumin; lukewarm baths, wet dressings, mild topical corticosteroids and bland emollients; oral antihistamine; antibiotics for signs of secondary infection; skin biopsy, with DIF if a blistering or connective tissue disease is possible; treat the cause (psoriasis, eczema, drugs, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
nodes.why: Erythroderma can be life-threatening and may need admission; care centers on monitoring and keeping metabolic and hemodynamic stability, because uncontrolled erythroderma brings electrolyte imbalance, dehydration and low protein. Symptoms are treated with lukewarm baths, wet dressings, mild topical corticosteroids, bland emollients and oral antihistamines; antibiotics are for signs of secondary infection; and the underlying cause is found and treated. A biopsy helps find the cause, but it does not replace the admission.

orders.dose: When severe; monitor and keep metabolic and hemodynamic stability; electrolyte imbalance, dehydration and low protein can become life-threatening
Bed rest, lukewarm baths, wet dressings, mild topical corticosteroids and bland emollients; oral antihistamines may help
For findings of secondary infection
Histopathology, with DIF for bullous or connective tissue disease; ESR and CRP raised in most
Preexisting dermatoses (psoriasis about half in some series, eczema), drugs (antiepileptics, sulfonamides, penicillins, vancomycin, lithium, allopurinol), malignancy such as CTCL; some idiopathic

nodes.summary: Erythroderma: admission when severe, protection of fluids, electrolytes and temperature, soothing skin care, and a search for the cause, psoriasis and eczema most often, then drugs and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Fever with low blood pressure and diffuse redness is the toxic shock route at the front door.

Fever and a rash after a tick risk: doxycycline now, as on the rickettsial route, even while the spots blanch. Fever with a spotty rash and no new drug: this pathway carries only the ED flags; the children's pathways are not built yet, and other causes in adults, such as secondary syphilis, are not in this version. Measles: isolate on arrival, tell infection control, notify public health on suspicion, care is supportive, and vitamin A is given for 2 days. Scarlet fever: penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days, away from school until 24 hours of antibiotics. Kawasaki disease: 5 days of fever with 4 of the 5 criteria, or coronary changes on echocardiography in an incomplete case, means admission for IVIG and aspirin, ideally within 7 to 10 days of fever onset.

Not a skin emergency: a local rash, or a widespread blanching rash in a well patient with normal bloods and no mucosal signs, often a simple drug or viral exanthem. Stop a suspect drug, treat the itch with a topical steroid and an oral antihistamine, and return for fever, blisters, mouth sores, facial swelling or a spreading rash. Not in this version: burns, bites and stings, scabies, impetigo, chronic dermatoses and secondary syphilis.

nodes.ask: Vesicles. What decides the plan?
options: Their spread, the eye and nose tip, immune status, pregnancy and eczema beneath
A Tzanck smear first; start an antiviral once it shows multinucleated giant cells
Vesicle PCR first, with an antiviral held back until the result is positive
Oral steroids first to settle the inflammation, then decide on an antiviral
nodes.chainStep: Map the spread (one dermatome, adjacent dermatomes, or scattered); look at the forehead, eyelid and nose tip and ask about eye pain or blurred vision; ask about immunosuppression and pregnancy; look for eczema beneath punched-out erosions; check the mouth, hands and feet; vesicle PCR when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient is immunocompromised
nodes.why: The plan turns on distribution and host. Zoster in one dermatome is treated by mouth; vesicles on the nose tip (the Hutchinson sign) mark nasociliary involvement and strongly predict eye complications; more than 20 lesions outside the primary and adjacent dermatomes is dissemination, and immunocompromise or dissemination means IV aciclovir; pregnancy changes the chickenpox plan; and punched-out erosions on eczema are eczema herpeticum. PCR is the most reliable test and the Tzanck smear is less sensitive and specific, but antivirals are not delayed for a definitive diagnosis. Systemic corticosteroids are not routinely recommended in zoster.

Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose: nasociliary involvement, which strongly predicts ocular complications
PCR of vesicle fluid is the most reliable test; the Tzanck smear is less sensitive and specific

Referral is mandatory when ocular involvement is suspected

Chickenpox, adult or pregnant, rash under 24 hours; crops, immunocompetent
Chickenpox, other; a well child, or an adult after 24 hours
